q: A Stellenbosch estate on the Simonsberg foothills is the reference point for Pinotage and also bottles a Bordeaux blend called Paul Sauer. Which estate?
exp: Its old bush-vine Pinotage is what people mean when they argue the grape can be serious, and the style has been held steady for decades. Paul Sauer carries the name of the family who planted the property and is built on Cabernet Sauvignon.

q: Between Valence and Montelimar the vines all but vanish for some fifty kilometres. What does that empty stretch separate?
opts: The Northern Rhone from the Southern Rhone
exp: The gap is why the two halves feel like different countries. North of it the climate is continental and the vineyards are steep; south of it the land opens out and the climate turns Mediterranean.

q: Harsh winters, a real risk of spring frost and a short season in which everything must ripen. Which climate type does the northern half of the valley have?
exp: Vintage variation matters far more in the north than in the south. A cool year gives lean, peppery Syrah and a warm one gives something much riper, from the same rows of vines.

q: Slopes so steep that no tractor can work them force growers to tie each vine to its own wooden pole. What is that pole called?
exp: The stakes are often lashed into tripods so the vine can resist the wind on an exposed terrace. Everything on those slopes, including the harvest, is carried by hand.

q: Almost every cru of the northern valley sits on the right bank of the river. Which two look back at them from the left?
exp: The hill of Hermitage and the flatter land around it are the exception, which is part of why Hermitage catches so much sun: the river swings west there and the hill ends up facing due south.

q: Red wine in every northern appellation that makes one must be built on a single black grape. Which one?
exp: One grape across the five northern appellations that make red is what makes the north such a clear lesson in site. Condrieu, Chateau-Grillet and Saint-Peray are white only. Grenache and Mourvedre belong to the south and are not permitted in any northern cru.

q: Whole clusters of a white grape may legally go into the fermenter alongside the Syrah in that northernmost cru. Which white grape?
exp: The two are often interplanted, so the practice began as a matter of convenience rather than theory. Picked together they also ripen together, which is why the tradition survived.

q: Cote-Rotie growers co-ferment only a little Viognier in practice, though the rules permit a good deal more. What is the legal ceiling?
exp: Most growers use nothing like the maximum, and many use none at all. A few percent is enough to change the aroma without turning the wine pale.

q: Local legend divides the hill above Ampuis between a landowner's two daughters, one fair and one dark. What are the two sectors called?
opts: The Cote des Blancs and the Cote des Noirs
exp: The story is charming and the geology is real: the two flanks genuinely differ in rock and in soil colour, and the wines differ with them.

q: Iron-rich schist and clay on one flank, paler granitic gneiss on the other. Which flank gives the sturdier, slower-maturing wine?
opts: The alluvial flat beside the river
exp: Brune builds tannin and needs time; Blonde is the more perfumed and open of the two. Many bottlings blend both, precisely to get the perfume and the frame together.

q: Apricot, honeysuckle and a broad oily texture with notably low acidity, from granite terraces just south of Ampuis. Which appellation is in the glass?
exp: Low acidity is the signature and the problem: the wine is glorious at two or three years and rarely rewards keeping. Picking date decides everything, since the aromatics arrive very late and the acid falls away fast.

q: An estate of barely more than three hectares holds an entire appellation to itself, enclosed within the boundaries of Condrieu. Which appellation?
exp: One of the smallest appellations in France, a single south-facing granite amphitheatre planted to Viognier. A whole appellation in one owner's hands is very nearly unique in the country.

q: Fermenting the white grapes together with the black, rather than blending two finished wines, achieves what?
exp: Compounds from the white grape bind to the red pigments and hold them in solution, so the wine ends up more stable in colour rather than paler. A lift in aroma comes with it, which is the part you can smell.

q: A single granite hill rising behind the town of Tain gives Syrah its most age-worthy expression in France. Which appellation crowns it?
exp: The hill is small enough to walk across in an hour and has been famous for centuries. Its reds were once shipped north and west to strengthen thinner wines, including claret, which tells you how concentrated they were.

q: Long-lived whites from that hill, capable of decades in bottle, are built on which pair of varieties?
exp: They close up for years in the middle of their life and then reopen, nutty and honeyed. A guest who opens one at five years old will usually think it dull.

q: Growers on the hill above Tain keep one parcel at its western end, a spine of hard granite under almost no topsoil, for their firmest and slowest-maturing red. Which parcel is that?
exp: Bare granite means small crops and tannin that arrives hard and fine, so wine from there needs the longest in bottle. Les Greffieux sits lower on clay and gravel and gives perfume and suppleness instead, while Les Rocoules is the parcel growers reserve for white.
